versions.title: Two gold lions on red
versions.note: Attributed later: Coats of arms only appear in Europe in the 1130s and 1140s. Heralds gave William these lions afterwards.

versions.title: Attributed arms
versions.note: Given to Stephen by later heralds. No arms he actually used survive.

versions.title: Three lions
versions.note: Three gold lions on red, first seen on Richard I's great seal of 1198. Still the arms of England today.

versions.title: England and France
versions.note: Edward III claimed the French throne in 1340 and put France's lilies in the place of honour.

versions.title: England and France
versions.note: Henry IV kept Edward III's arms at first.

versions.title: France modern
versions.note: Around 1406 the lilies were cut to three, copying the French kings' own change.

versions.title: Red rose badge
versions.note: A Lancastrian badge, made famous mostly after the fact by the Tudors.

versions.title: Royal arms
versions.note: The same royal arms as Lancaster: the war was over who bore them.

versions.title: White rose badge
versions.note: The white rose of the House of York.

versions.title: Royal arms
versions.note: Unchanged from Lancaster and York; the Tudors changed the supporters (dragon, greyhound, lion) beside the shield.

versions.title: Tudor rose
versions.note: Henry VII joined the red rose and the white after marrying Elizabeth of York.

versions.title: Jane Grey's own arms
versions.note: Her family arms, joining her father's Grey line and her mother's Brandon line.

versions.title: England, Scotland and Ireland
versions.note: James I added Scotland's lion and Ireland's harp: the first arms of all three kingdoms. Paused 1649 to 1660.

versions.title: Great Britain
versions.note: After the Union of 1707 England and Scotland share one quarter.

versions.title: Commonwealth
versions.note: No crown and no lions: St George's cross for England and the harp for Ireland.

versions.title: Protectorate
versions.note: Cromwell's own black lion sits at the centre of the three kingdoms.

versions.title: Stuart arms with Nassau
versions.note: William of Orange put the lion of Nassau in a small shield at the centre.

versions.title: Hanover quarter
versions.note: George I added his German lands in the fourth quarter. France's lilies stayed until 1801.

versions.title: United Kingdom and Hanover
versions.note: France was finally dropped in 1801; Hanover sits in the centre, crowned as a kingdom from 1816.

versions.title: Victoria
versions.note: As a woman Victoria could not inherit Hanover, so it left the arms: the version still used today.

versions.title: Royal arms
versions.note: Edward VII kept Victoria's royal arms unchanged.

versions.title: Royal arms
versions.note: The family renamed itself Windsor in 1917; the arms did not change.

versions.title: Elizabeth II
versions.note: The same arms under St Edward's Crown. Charles III restored the Tudor crown shape.

versions.title: Arms of France
versions.note: Prince Louis bore the French royal arms: gold lilies scattered on blue.

scotland/alpin.none: No arms: Coats of arms only appear in Europe in the 1130s and 1140s. Scotland's lion appears only in the 1220s.

scotland/moray.none: No arms: Coats of arms only appear in Europe in the 1130s and 1140s.

versions.title: Lion rampant
versions.note: The red lion first appears on Alexander II's seal around 1222; the double border of lilies came later in the century. Earlier kings of this house had no arms.

versions.title: Balliol family arms
versions.note: The Balliols' own arms: a white border-shape (an orle) on red.

versions.title: Royal arms
versions.note: As king, John bore the lion of Scotland.

versions.title: Bruce family arms
versions.note: A red saltire on gold, the arms of the Bruces of Annandale.

versions.title: Royal arms
versions.note: Crowned in 1306, Robert took the lion of Scotland.

versions.title: Royal arms
versions.note: The Stewarts kept the lion and its border of lilies.

versions.title: Three kingdoms, Scottish version
versions.note: After 1603 Scotland's lion takes the first quarter in the version used in Scotland.

versions.title: France ancient
versions.note: Gold lilies scattered on blue, first in full on Prince Louis's seal of 1211. The first Capetians had no arms: Coats of arms only appear in Europe in the 1130s and 1140s.

versions.title: France ancient
versions.note: The Valois kept the scattered lilies at first.

versions.title: France modern
versions.note: Around 1376 Charles V cut the lilies to three, said to honour the Trinity.

versions.title: England and France
versions.note: Henry VI, crowned in Paris in 1431, bore the joint arms of both crowns.

versions.title: France and Navarre
versions.note: Henry IV was already King of Navarre, so its gold chains on red sit beside the lilies.

versions.title: Restoration
versions.note: The restored Bourbons brought back the three lilies.

france/republic.none: No arms: the Revolution abolished coats of arms in 1790. The Republic used emblems such as Marianne and the fasces instead.

versions.title: First Empire
versions.note: Napoleon swapped the lilies for a Roman-style gold eagle on blue, with golden bees on the mantle.

versions.title: Second Empire
versions.note: Napoleon III revived his uncle's eagle.

versions.title: July Monarchy
versions.note: Louis-Philippe dropped the lilies for the 1830 Charter, a constitution, in the centre.

versions.title: Attributed arms
versions.note: Invented centuries later: half the imperial eagle, half France's lilies. Coats of arms only appear in Europe in the 1130s and 1140s.

hre/ottonian.none: No arms: emperors of this era used seals, crosses and the Holy Lance. The eagle became a fixed emblem only under the Hohenstaufen.

hre/salian.none: No arms: Coats of arms only appear in Europe in the 1130s and 1140s. The Salians sealed with their portraits instead.

hre/supplinburg.none: No arms: Coats of arms only appear in Europe in the 1130s and 1140s.

versions.title: Imperial eagle
versions.note: A black single-headed eagle on gold: the emblem of the Empire itself, fixed in this period.

versions.title: Hohenstaufen Sicily
versions.note: The black eagle on white the family used as kings of Sicily.

versions.title: Otto IV
versions.note: Half the imperial eagle, half the English lions of his uncle Richard I, as drawn by Matthew Paris.

versions.title: Habsburg family arms
versions.note: A red lion on gold: the counts of Habsburg in Switzerland.

versions.title: Rudolf I
versions.note: The first Habsburg king put his lion on the imperial eagle.

versions.title: Double-headed eagle
versions.note: From 1433 emperors bore a two-headed eagle. The Habsburgs held it, with one break, until 1806.

versions.title: Nassau
versions.note: A gold lion among gold billets on blue: Adolf's family, later the house of Orange-Nassau.

versions.title: Charles IV
versions.note: The imperial eagle with Bohemia's white lion, his first crown.

versions.title: Double-headed eagle
versions.note: Sigismund introduced the two-headed eagle when crowned emperor in 1433.

versions.title: Bavarian lozenges
versions.note: The blue and white lozenges of Bavaria, still the state's colours. Charles VII bore them again in 1742 to 1745.

versions.title: Lorraine
versions.note: A red bend with three white eaglets (alerions) on gold.

versions.title: Habsburg-Lorraine
versions.note: Habsburg's lion, Austria's red-white-red and Lorraine's bend: the new joint house of Maria Theresa and Francis.
